utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to follow me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm going to go through your background information and just ask you if you could confirm it. You were born on 20th December, 1959, in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You are of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You grew up in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1979 you moved to Zagreb and worked there as a carpenter until January 1991 when you were hired as a regular police officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for your benefit I would like to refer the Court to atlas, which is Exhibit 23, and specifically to page 20 of the atlas, and at A4 you can see where village of Saborsko is located. It is at the bottom -- left bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, can you tell the Judges, about how many households were there in Saborsko? And I am referring to the year 1990, beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were 300 house numbers. As for the population, well, about 600, 700.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Saborsko, was it a Croat village or a Serb village or did it have a mixed population?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most were Croat and there were six or seven houses that were Serb since time immemorial. So they were ethnic Serbs and they lived there, and then there were those that came from Sisak, Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us in the vicinity or nearby of Saborsko, were there any other purely Croat villages or predominantly inhabited villages by Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was on the other side, towards Lake Plitvice; Poljanak and some other villages, Seci Poljana, the neighbouring village, first, and then Poljanak was second.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about Serb villages? Can you tell us what Serb villages were nearby Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the other side, towards Ogulin, was Licka Jasenica first, then Blato, Plavca Draga, Haski, and Latin Vojnivac [phoen]. Those were Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how would you describe the atmosphere, the situation, in Saborsko? How did you -- how did people get along? And again I'm referring to 1990 -- 1990, beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we got along. People from Jasenica went to our school in fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth grade because they had school only through the fourth grade. So we agreed -- we got along very well, and we would even spend the night at each other's house. For example, one of my classmates spent nights at my house and I spent nights at his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Without going into any more details, was there a time when this atmosphere changed, this good relationship?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that it changed that much that we were quarrelling or fighting or something like that. Quite simply, it was cut off and you couldn't pass through Jasenica and Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said it was cut off. Do you know who cut it off?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1992 -- no, 1991, when the war started raging in Pakrac, Petrinja, wherever, I wasn't really following this all this much. So we couldn't pass through from Saborsko to Ogulin. It's on the other side. The bus didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I only wanted to know whether you know who cut it off, whether there were any soldiers, paramilitary, police, whether it was -- who cut it off? If you do not know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Quite simply, the regular bus to Ogulin went at ten past 5.00 in the morning and it came back from Jasenica. That was it. I don't know who returned it, and then it never came back. It went via Slunj to Ogulin and it never came back. This bus line no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let's go back to the time you became a policeman. You -- do you remember when you were hired exactly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: 14th or the 15th of January. I'm not sure. I think it's the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After you were hired, did you take any training?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to Simunska, to some course in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after you took part in this training, what was your assignment? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Ogulin I was sent to Plaski. There was some station there, or rather, an outpost in Plasko, and then I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who was your commander? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ogulin, Ante Vujovic, he was the main commander; and in Plasko, Dusan Latas, the commander of that outpost.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Plasko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think about 20 days. I'm not sure exactly when I came there to Plaski. I'm not sure of the date, but I worked there until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand the date. Can you please repeat it, approximately until when.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 26th of February. I think that's the way it was. That was the last day that I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened? What made you -- what made you to leave this place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the patrol. I don't know. The battery of the Motorola, of the hand-held radio, was in the functioning properly, and then we went back to the station to get a new battery, I and Ilija Celina, a policeman from Blato, we were together. And at that moment Olga Solaja, I think, came, a lady dentist from Plitvica. Now, was it -- or rather, Dusan Latas said that we should come there, that the -- that Olga Solaja and Martic's men came and were asking us to sign documents saying that we would work for the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you sign this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Dusan, the commander, called us -- there were a lot of them in a small room, and then we were standing at the door and I said that I couldn't sign it, that I had just signed something for the Croatian police. And he said: All right. There is no place for you here, then. And he said to Ilija, and Ilija also didn't want to sign. So then we left -- or rather, they told us to go to Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This Krajina Police, what did you know about this Krajina Police? Who did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard - I don't know - I didn't see anyone -- or rather, I hadn't seen anyone until then. They had some kind of training somewhere near Knin, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You didn't know what Krajina Police was, who did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were saying it was Martic's police, nothing else. Now, who was there and how -- well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you go from Plaski?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To Ogulin, to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the date was exactly. Until Easter, until that policeman got killed in Plitvice. And that day we left and we did not return. We couldn't get through any longer to Saborski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you say that you couldn't get any longer to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I meant from Saborski back. That day we got through in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak clearly into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The interpreters just ask if you could speak a little bit more clear -- clearer to the microphones. They have a hard time to understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Probably louder, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And a little bit louder. In Saborsko, what did you do in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the telephones were working and we called Ogulin and they told us to remain in Saborsko. We, the policemen who were living in Saborsko, should remain in Saborsko. So we did stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you establish a police station?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then they came through Slunj and established a sort of police station there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Approximately how many policemen were there in Saborsko at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 27 or 8 active policemen, and about four or five reserve policemen. I think that the total was 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, of course, and pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity somewhere? You said earlier: "Then they came through Slunj and established a sort of police station there." Who are the "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not from Slunj but via Slunj. From Ogulin. There was a number of members of special units and the commander there, and they came along this road without any asphalt. So Ante Vujovic and these men came to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, who are "they," these people who came through Slunj? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander from Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The commander of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Krajina Police or Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to clarify, so there were regular police, these 28 regular policemen, including you, plus this special police unit. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The special one came with the commander and then they stayed for eight or ten days, I don't know, and then they went back, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They went back to Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To Ogulin, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after they left, you stayed there alone, I mean these 28 policemen.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were your tasks as a policeman in Saborsko at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They held -- we held these check-points in case of an attack - during the day two policemen, and during the night three - at the village and at the end of Saborsko towards Licka Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell us, were there any military facilities in that area? And I am referring to JNA --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko, no, but in Licka Jasenica and up there where the railroad went, where the train went, that's where there was a barracks of the JNA. And the training grounds were on the other side of Saborsko, the military training grounds of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did JNA soldiers or JNA vehicles, did they pass through Saborsko at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They did. They would pass with two armoured vehicles, APCs, from Plitvica and Licka Jasenica. They said it was some kind of patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How often did they pass through Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They would start out from Plitvica at about 10 a.m. to Licka Jasenica, and I don't know whether they went to Plaski or where they went but they went in that direction, downhill, and then in the afternoon they would come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question was: How often? It means was it every day, every week, or just once a month?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Every day they went through, and when the shelling started, then the elderly women and the men went out onto the road and wouldn't let them through, and they said: Don't shoot. And then an old woman had a part of a hand-grenade of an 82-millimetre hand-grenade, and she showed it to the JNA, and she said: This is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you say after the shelling started, which date are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very hard to say what the date was. When that happened on the 5th of August, the shelling, I mean, after that people didn't pass through -- they didn't pass through every day but every fifth or sixth day after those people stopped them there. But nobody touched them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So before 5th of August, they were able to pass through your village. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they used to pass through every day. But later on it wasn't so often; it was every five or six days, not every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to this event on 5th of August. When the shelling started, what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 9.00 in the morning, or 8.30. I can't be precise about the time, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you at the time of that attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At the check-point towards Licka Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Preceding the attack on Saborsko, were any ultimatums or demands made by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there anything which would indicate that the shelling would start on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was nothing to foreshadow the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did the shellings last that day, the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't one shell after the other. They would launch a few shells and then there would be an interval, and then they would launch a few more. And then this went on for a long time, until the afternoon. There would be a 15-minute lull, maybe, and then it would resume again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you manage to count how many shells fell on Saborsko that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 150, maybe more. We wrote that down. The commander, Slavko Ceranic, wrote it down, and I did, too, but it all remained there, it's all been burnt, so I can't remember everything precisely. But there were a lot. I'm sure there were at least 150, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the time the shelling started or during the time of shelling, did you put up any defence? Did you try to fight back?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have anything to fire with except our rifles and pistols. We didn't have mortars or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At that time the shelling started on the 5th of August, was there any other unit, apart from your regular police unit? Were there any special units, Croatian special units?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was this special unit from Duga Resa. They were stationed in the school in case there was some kind of attack, in order for them to help and to have some kind of defence line established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they establish a defence line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They did, but then they fled towards Slunj by night. At around 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening they abandoned everything and only we were left behind, the police, in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the 5th of August -- during the shelling, did you see whether any houses were damaged?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: One or two houses were hit, and the other shells landed next to the houses. Quite a lot of them fell on the cemetery and around the cemetery. I don't know what they were aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you try to communicate with Serbs about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't. We didn't have electricity or anything; we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. The question was: Did you try to communicate with the Serbs? I think this is very generalised. Perhaps the term "the attackers" could be used. I think that the way this term was used is not correct. If somebody is attacking, it's a unit. It can be comprised of members of the Serbian ethnicity or another ethnicity, but they are not Serbs, they are attackers. We can get an explanation as to whether they were Territorial Defence or a military unit of volunteers, the JNA, or somebody else. In order to make myself clear, a few days ago the Israeli army attacked a prison in Palestine, but nobody says "the Jews attacked the prison," they say "the Israeli army." If somebody said "the Jews attacked," it would cause a scandal. I don't want such language to be used here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that when Mr. Milovancevic stands up to object, you take your seat. Okay. And then when he finishes, you can stand up. Do you have any answer to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to now clarify who attacked the Saborsko village. And I know that I was not specific enough when establishing who were the attackers when using the expression "Serbs." So if I may, I will clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, at the time of the attack or any time later, did you learn who attacked you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we could only imagine who it was, whether it was a paramilitary unit or the JNA. But we knew by the mortar it was the JNA, but who was using it on the other side we couldn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I will repeat the question: Did you try to communicate with anybody or did you try to find out who -- with whom you could communicate to stop the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't. How could we? We had no electricity, no telephone lines, everything had to go through Ogulin and by way of Plasko, but it was all cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because you mentioned during your testimony that at one point during the shelling you stopped a senior soldier, a JNA soldier, and a woman from your village showed him shrapnel or part of some -- some hand-grenade. Do you remember this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the reaction of this person when you showed him -- or this woman showed him the remains of the -- of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. He stood there and looked at it and she showed it to him and she said: It says JNA here. Are you the JNA? And he said: Yes. And nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to the civilians on 5th of August? Did they stay in the village or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They went through Rakovica, through the forest. Some of them went by tractor, or I don't know how they went, and they went to Grabovac, and the Red Cross came there with two or three buses. And then the children and the elderly women were taken away to Crikvenica at the seaside. I don't know who escorted them there. And as for the others, some came back on the first day and the others came back on the second day, from Grabovac to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After 5th of August, or after some of them returned, can you tell -- estimate approximately how many civilians stayed in that village after 6th, 7th, 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- after they returned from where?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The witness said that, "As for the others, some came back on the first day and some came back on the second day, from Grabovac to Saborsko."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So after they returned -- some returned, you said, so approximately how many civilians still stayed in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think about 400 came back. I don't know how many got onto those two or three buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that this special unit from Duga Resa left the same night, the same night of 5th of August. Did you try -- did you try to get some other assistance, some other help from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning I went to Slunj, and I asked Commander Panic to let a few policemen go, 15 or 20, to come and help us so that there would be more of us if we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know, these people from Slunj, what kind of weapon did they bring with them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Rifles and pistols like ours. And they were each issued with 60 pieces of ammunition. I don't know exactly how much ammunition they had, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did this unit stay in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: 10, 12, 15 days. It was at least 10, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any time in September, did you receive any significant help? And I'm relating to manpower or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Zagreb a convoy arrived through Lipice, Glibodol, and then by the forest road through Javornik and then on to Saborsko. It was an unasphalted road going through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know how many people formed this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About a hundred or 110, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were these people? Were they policemen or civilian? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These were all people from Saborsko who had been working in Rijeka, Zagreb, or Split. They gathered together in Zagreb - I don't know who called them together - and then they came to Saborsko to help. They brought food, cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they bring any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They brought sub-machine-guns and -- the old ones, and two mortars - I think there were two mortars - and an anti-aircraft gun of some kind. I'm not sure what it's called technically.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On the way from -- on the way you describe from Saborsko, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were holding the line, and I don't know whether they were paramilitaries or someone else in Glibodol, they captured eight or nine of those people who were coming from Zagreb. Some were younger and some were older. There was an elderly man. I think his name was Milan Boca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that they -- that they captured people who were coming from Zagreb. Is it correct or misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those people who are going from Zagreb captured somebody. There was a check-point above Licka Jasenica-Glibodol, and then the road goes on to Dabar. There was a kind of check-point there. I don't know what kind of unit was manning it and who they belonged to. They belonged to the other side, from Licka Jasenica, but I don't know whether it was a company or what kind of company or who it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were these people who were captured; what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew two of them; Dusko Jovicic and Damir Vorkapic. They used to work with us in the police. Jovicic was in the police before and Damir Vorkapic, from Plasko, signed up the same day I did in the policija, which is the Croatian police, on the 15th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These captured people, were they brought to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw them. They were sitting there in a room at the police station. This commander who came from Zagreb to be the commander in Saborsko, he was the one who was talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These captured people, did you notice whether they wore any patches on their clothes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all wearing civilian clothes, but they just had weapons when they were taken prisoner. Damir Vorkapic -- well, they had -- they -- Damir and Dusko Jovicic had jeans and also they wore these camouflage uniforms on top of the jeans with this patch of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean a patch of Krajina? Can you be a little bit more specific. How -- how did it look like?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was sitting there but I didn't go into the room because the commander was talking to them. So you could see this one thing - now, how should I put this? - a two-headed eagle. I don't know. I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know to what unit, what unit they belonged to, these patches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Vorkapic and Jovicic worked in the police. They signed up for Krajina, that they would work for them. So they stayed in Plaski. So I think they were the milicija, the police of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did these captured people stay in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not say exactly how long, but there was an exchange because there were three from Drezni Grad who were taken prisoner somewhere near Slunj. And they were taken to Plaski, and then the nine were exchanged for those three. The commander of the war unit coordinated all of that, sent this young man who had been taken prisoner to go to Jasenica, and he sent some letter. And then the young man came back, and then in the evening at 5.00 there was an exchange, the same day or the following day. I'm not sure. I don't know exactly. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So these nine Serbs were exchanged for three, and these three, which ethnicity did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After or during that exchange, was -- were there any arrests?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think it was the same time, 5.00 or 6.00 in the evening. Because when you go from Saborsko to Rakovica along the forest path, Vlado Vukovic, Ivica Vukovic, or Ivan - I don't know what his real name is - were taken prisoner -- it's Ivan or Ivica. And then a Bosnian who wanted to go to Kladusa. He was from Kladusa but he came from Zagreb with those who were from Saborsko. He wanted to go to Kladusa to see his wife and children. So the three of them were taken prisoner. That's what I heard. We didn't know where they had been. That's what we heard later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- I understand you weren't there when they were arrested. Did you hear or did you learn from -- from somebody else who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know exactly who was there and what happened and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. If it is convenient to you, then we will take a break, come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, before the break we were talking about the circumstances of arrival of this convoy of people from Zagreb and Rijeka to Saborsko. Do you know who was the commander of these people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Krizmanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These 100 people, plus-minus, did they form any unit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: War Unit Saborsko, something like that. I think that's what they called themselves. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did they put up any effective resistance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they took up positions around Saborsko, as the commander had ordered. That's what they did, and that's the way it was for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For a while. For how long?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Until Saborsko fell. When was that? That was the 12th of November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We will talk about events of 12th of November. I would like to return now to these shellings. The shellings started on 5th of August. Did the shelling continue also in September?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, until the attack, until Saborsko fell. Not every day, but every other day or one day a bit and then the next day there would be more shells, more shelling, and they would attack from Poljanak, from the direction of Plitvica. There was this one attack, I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean one attack from Poljanak? What do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From the side of Poljanak, from Plitvica, there was some shooting from there. And then those who were up there -- I was not up there, but I just know that there were attacks in order to get through to take Kuselj. Kuselj is a hamlet that also belongs to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened in Kuselj? Was it attacked?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not attacked because that line was there, at the end of Kuselj. And then they repelled the attack but there were wounded and killed persons on our part, among us from Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether during September/October some other Croat villages or hamlets were attacked? And to be more specific, of course I am talking about the region or the area surrounding Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Saborsko was not attacked that way, I mean not from the side of Plitvica. It was mortar shells, things like that. Only this one attack was direct, the end of September/beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any -- or were there any air attacks, either on Saborsko or any other village in that region?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Once there was an attack: One aircraft was firing rockets at the area around the cemetery, and then it left. And then later, in the beginning of November, I think, again there was a rocket attack on Kuselj, and then some young men got killed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also stated that when the shelling started there were no -- there was no significant damage done to the buildings in Saborsko. What about later, where you said the shelling continued until the 12th of November? Did any damage was done at the later stage?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, yes, especially when this convoy from Zagreb came. Now, was it on the 23rd or the 25th of September? That's when the church and the school were hit and some houses. When shells fell nearby, then windows were broken and facades were damaged, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In October, did you receive any further assistance; manpower, ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one convoy came, but it wasn't manpower, it was food; flour, cigarettes, fruit juice, things like that, whatever they brought. I know about cigarettes, though; we did get cigarettes and flour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I would like to talk about 12th of November. What happened on 12th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of November I wasn't there -- now -- well, I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you on 12th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the 12th of December, though?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, the 12th of November. Yes, yes, yes. In Ogulin. I left Saborsko. On the 9th of November I went to Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why did you go to Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of November I didn't come back. Saborsko fell on the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why did you go to Ogulin on 9th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of this wartime unit, Marko Krizmanic, sent me and some other men. And there were these two men, one from Lipice and one from Slunj, went to Zagreb, wherever -- or actually, he went to Zagreb from Ogulin. And he said that there were these men from Slunj who were supposed to pass through Glibodol, that we should go there to help them go via Glibodol and that they would go to Slunj on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And who were these men? Were they soldiers? Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: People from Slunj who lived in Zagreb, Karlovac, Rijeka, who also wanted to go to Slunj to help, because until then there had been no fighting in Slunj so they wanted to sort of help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you stated on 12th of November Saborsko fell. How did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then we were supposed to go back from Ogulin with this convoy from Slunj, the one that was from Slunj. We were supposed to go towards Lipice and towards Glibodol, and I don't know, some soldiers, some officer, whoever -- well, anyway, a military man got out and stood there by the traffic light. He got out from the barracks, and he said that no one could pass through because Saborsko was falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This war unit, was it still in Saborsko at the time, on 12th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed there when I left, and then they went through Bosnia, wherever. As people were fleeing, they left, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, this war unit, did they launch any attacks or did they defend the area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Saborsko? In Saborsko they were defending.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And somewhere else? Did they launch any attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The war unit and the police, we were just in Saborsko, within the perimeter of Saborsko. We didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just to really make it sure that we all understood: This war unit, who were the people who were in war unit? Were they professional soldiers? Professional policemen?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were people who had worked in the police before, too, 10 or 15 years or something like that. And then they joined the police in 1990, and then there were civilians who were doing some kind of civilian work. It was sort of the reserve force of the MUP. They all belonged to the reserve force of the MUP, I mean the other ones did. The reserve, the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that you learned that Saborsko fell. So after you learned that Saborsko fell, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they said that there were civilians in Lipice near Brinje, that's a hamlet out there. And then I and this man -- well, I don't know. And then this man from Ogulin, and he said: Let's go and see who's there. And then when we got there, there were these women and the elderly from Saborsko. And my mother was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did your mother tell you what happened in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I saw that my father wasn't there, and I said: Where is dad? And he -- and she said: They killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did she tell you who killed him, how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were in a cellar, men and women, and then they stood outside in front of a house. The women were put on one side and the men on another side, and then the women were let go, they could go into the forest there towards Glibodol, and as for the men, they shot them, killed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did your mother mention who did it? Were -- who killed your father; were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in uniforms, she said, olive-green-grey, like the JNA. When I did my military service in the JNA, that kind of uniform, and camouflage, multi-coloured. I don't know, mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At that time, did you learn, did you receive any information that there were more people killed, apart from your father?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, seven of them altogether. There were seven in that place and all seven were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know their age, how old were they? Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians. My father was born in 1931. He was 60. The others were perhaps a year older or a year younger than him, but they had all been born around 1930 or 1931.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: From Lipice, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Back to Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there a time when you come back to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1995, did -- did you come back to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, after Operation Storm. Then the army went first and the police came as far as Plasko, following the army. And then we, the police, took the police station in Plasko and we were given assignments as to which buildings to guard. Every policeman was given an assignment. And after that, on the second day, we got as far as Licka Jasenica and we stationed ourselves there, and the commander organised guard duty. Everything had to be guarded, but there was always a policeman near the church and near the school and such important buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any Orthodox church in Licka Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there a Catholic church in Licka Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In which state did you find the Orthodox church in Licka Jasenica? Was it damaged?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't damaged. It looked just as it had looked before the war when I visited Jasenica. We used to go there from Saborsko when there was some kind of event there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at some point did you come back to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't until we got approval. And then we went back to Saborsko and there was nothing to see there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean? How did the village look like when you -- when you went -- when you returned there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the houses had been made of wood and they had been set on fire. The houses that were made of brick, as well as the school and the church, had all been destroyed, and only the ruins were still standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the time you were in Saborsko - and I am referring to the time in 1995 after you returned - apart from destroyed houses and church, did you also find something else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, when we were looking for the people who had been killed, we searched for their graves. Some people who remained in Jasenica, elderly people, told us what they knew of the burial sites, and then we went to search for them. In some places the graves were marked and in others they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what -- what did you find? Did you remain -- did you find some remains, some corpses?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was afterwards. General Grujic from Zagreb - I don't really know whether he's a general - there was an exhumation and he used to come with his team and he would do the exhumation and we would just guard the sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were present during the exhumation. Did you yourself manage to identify any bodies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't -- you would know more or less where people had been when they were killed, but an elderly man from Licka Jasenica told us that the civilians had all been thrown into a pit, and that's how we knew. And those who had been killed at certain positions were buried right there, where they fell in the sand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many bodies were found in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact number. I never even thought about it. I can only guess: Three in one place, five in another, seven in yet another place. Maybe I could add them up, but I didn't attend the last two or three exhumations, so I couldn't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During this exhumation, was the body of your father found?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am Defence counsel for Milan Martic. This is the stage of your testimony where the Defence will put questions to you. This is the so-called cross-examination. Therefore, I will ask you some questions. As we both understand each other and the interpreters have to interpret both my question and your reply, please make a pause between my question and your answer, and I will try to do the same. Thank you. You stated today that you finished primary school and two grades of secondary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in the late 1970s you went to Zagreb and worked until 1991 as a carpenter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that on the 15th of January, 1991, you got a job as a policeman in the Croatian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until the 15th of January, 1991, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had done your regular military service. Where were you assigned as a reservist? What were you as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "as a reservist"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to Vostarije, to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So your specialty was infantry?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that on the 15th of January you changed jobs and you stopped being a carpenter and became a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I thought I would have an easier time - it's all in the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb, my application to become a policeman - because I thought I would be at home. When I was working as a carpenter, I had to go on building sites all over Croatia. I had to be out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you applied because you saw the job advertised? How was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it -- in 1990 they were receiving policemen and then in early 1991 or late 1990 I applied. And I went for a medical examination and I was received into the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you were received into the police, had you completed some kind of police school before the 15th of January, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was sent for a course after I was employed as a policeman, a 15-day course in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this before you were received as a policeman or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was when I was received into the police that I was sent to the training course, and then in 1991 -- in 1990, when Saborsko fell, I went for another training course. And then I took exams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusion in the transcript, Saborsko, according to what we've heard from you just now, fell in 1991. Are you referring to that time, the year 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time when you applied to join the Croatian police, what was the official title of the Croatian police; was it "policija" or "redarstvo"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was still called the milicija, that's what it said, as before, the way it used to be, milicija. That's what it still said. And there was a star and everything when I applied to join the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you say that there was still a star, were there any changes after that; and what kind of changes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then - I don't know what month - there was the Croatian coat of arms, and the name was changed to policija. That was, I think, sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the name was changed from milicija to policija or to redarstvo?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It said policija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And when you -- please make a pause. When you mentioned the coat of arms, was it the chequer-board coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in your statement that when you were received into the police after the 15th of January, 1991, you went to the police training school in Zagreb. Was this the school in Sveto Simunska Street in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a course. It wasn't training. It was a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a course," are you referring to that 15-day course that you just mentioned a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at that time how many people were attending that school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Among those attending the school, were there those who had not been born in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that among those attending the first course there were 450 Croats from Western Herzegovina, from neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HDZ played any role in selecting those who would attend that course; that's the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I know what the HDZ is, but I don't know. I wrote out the application form in Ogulin to join the police, and from them I was -- I received a note saying that I should go to Zagreb for my medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will quote to you a statement by Perica Juric, who was the then-deputy minister of interior affairs, and it's a quotation from the book "The First Croatian Policeman" by Davor Runtic, and it reads as follows: "We worked at great speed and within a few days we managed to gather those people together. We worked in a way that was not the usual way. Word would be sent through the most prominent members of the HDZ and everything would proceed without problems. The jobs were open for everyone who wanted to apply. Sveto Simunska was open for anyone who arrived. Everybody was accepted. An offer was made to everyone to undergo training and to undergo the check that happened through the training. I wanted to say that the HDZ was the predominant party, although not the only one, that provided information to people." Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never engaged in politics and I don't follow politics to this day. I have nothing to say about this. I didn't read this book, I didn't even know this book existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you whether you had read the book but whether what you saw happening in that centre where you went for your 15-day training course, whether this corresponds to what the then-minister -- deputy minister of the interior says, that everyone who applied was received.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know some people who applied and were not received from Saborsko. They wanted to apply, they went there, but they were not received. That's how it was. It's not true that anyone who wanted could become a policeman. I can tell you the names of these people, their first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether among those attending the school were those who had a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. It's possible. How would I know? Perhaps they had had a traffic misdemeanour or something and served their punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will quote something else that Perica Juric says in this book "The First Croatian Policeman." I quote: "There were objections made to me personally because I initiated and carried out this whole programme. I was told there were those who had criminal records among them. I have to state a few facts here. The young Croatian authorities were not aware of the fact that a broad amnesty was needed. Every man needs to be given a second chance. That's how this group of first Croatian policemen came to include a small group of men who had to be given such a chance." Does this correspond to what you were able to see and hear and learn?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were taught criminology at the training course and we were taught how to behave on the road and so on, out on the beat, how to act, but -- you know, how -- what to do if there was a theft or a robbery. That's what the course was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Josip Boljkovac, says in his book "The First Croatian Policeman" that: "The course had been planned, that a curriculum had been elaborated that had to be dealt with, so in Sveto Simunska Street we are going to train five police battalions and no one noticed that we were actually creating an army there within the police." You mentioned that in Saborsko there was a war unit of Saborsko. Can this statement pertain to Saborsko as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the situation in Saborsko? They came from Zagreb, that's what they were called, the war unit. I don't know who sent them and whatever happened. I don't understand this. I don't see what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a group of about 100 to about 120 men had arrived from Zagreb and that originally they had come from Saborsko. All of them were reserve policemen. They were commanded by a man from Zagreb, and when they came to Saborsko they established a war unit of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: But they were established in Zagreb as a war unit, not in Saborsko, and that's how they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know about other things. I told you about what I saw and what I know. What do I know about books and things like that? What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on Easter 1991 you were deployed as a policeman in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We went from Saborsko to Ogulin. I was working on that -- or rather, from Ogulin I went to Saborsko and there were three or four of us. And then Ilija Celina from Blato, he's an ethnic Serb, he also came to Blato. And we went on and the bus went the next morning. I don't know who stopped it, whatever, but it was from Licka Jasenica. So that was it, as far as Ogulin was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this period of time as the period when Easter took place in 1991. Do you link Easter 1991 to what happened in Plitvica 1991? You said that there was a policeman killed in Plitvica then.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the only thing I said, that's when that happened. I came from Ogulin and the next day you could not take a bus back to Ogulin at 5.10 in the morning, which is when the bus usually went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave not to the Office of the Prosecutor but to the police, to the police station in Ogulin in 1994, and its number is 01510895 and the date is the 18th of April, 1994, in that record your statement is included and you signed it at the end. So in that statement you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you say, can you give him a copy and give the rest of the people in the court a copy, Mr. Milovancevic, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We don't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have copies of any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- So do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have copies for the interpreters? They said they don't have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment we don't have that, Your Honour. I think that our colleague from the OTP said that she had a copy, but we just prepared copies for the Trial Chamber. I'm just going to put a brief question. I just wanted to say something so this contains the statement given to the OTP in 2001 and behind it is the second part of the text, behind the English translation, the statement given to the police in Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just -- just a second, Mr. -- let's not hurry. I notice that you have given the Chamber a B/C/S and an English version. Maybe if we share with the translators and give them the B/C/S, because we don't understand the B/C/S, it might just help, and we can keep the English version. Would that help?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps it can be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of all booths. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is suggested that maybe if you put it on the ELMO, then everybody will see it who can read B/C/S. While we are at it, Mr. Milovancevic, and also the Prosecution, may I suggest that when we prepare copies, we think of the interpreters as well, copies for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I shall bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the monitor -- thank you. On the monitor, could you please show this statement, this record of taking a statement. That is document 01510895, the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness -- [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, there's -- just a second, Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, if you can refer us in the English version what page we must look at. The -- okay. I think I'm with you -- no, it's not in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to look only at the first page of this statement. We are not going to deal with the statements themselves because they're basically identical, the one given to the OTP and the one given to the Ogulin police station. I'm just interested in this first page of the statement given on the 18th of April, 1994. Yes, now on the monitor we see the record. So could you please put it up a bit so we see the end of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a statement that was given to the Karlovac police administration, the police station of Ogulin, and the date is the 18th of April, 1994, and it says that you gave this statement, and at the end of the first page -- do you recognise this statement? Have you seen this statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read the first page exactly when I read the -- when I made the statement, but when he wrote it all out, he gave it to me to sign, but I didn't read the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll also show you the last page, where your signature is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that I signed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the top left-land hand side of this page number 1 so that we see where the document comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third police station Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of this first page, it says: "On the 15th of January the same year, I joined the police. After becoming a member of the police, I worked at -- in the police station in Plaski until the 26th of February. And after that I worked in Saborsko -- or rather, until it was -- before Saborsko was established, and then I worked in Ogulin." Did you train?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe he meant something different, when I joined the police as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this last sentence. "At the beginning of the fourth month, April, an outpost in Saborsko was established when I was transferred to work there."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So until the month of April, there was no police outpost in Saborsko; that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This material will no longer be needed on the monitor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that at the newly established police outpost in Saborsko there were 32 policemen, four or five in the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact number now, but I think it was around that -- well, there were about 30, 32, something like that. I think it was 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated also that you, like all other members of the police outpost in Saborsko, were armed with pistols, which I assume are personal weapons, and active policemen had automatic rifles as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was an active policeman and I had a rifle and a pistol, whatever you were issued with when you joined the police. What else were you issued but that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This answer of yours, does that mean that 32 policemen were at the police station in Saborsko and that they all had automatic rifles in addition to pistols?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you said that you heard rumours that Martic's police was stopping people at check-points and that some were beaten up, too. Did you see this yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I saw it. I said that I heard it, sort of -- well, whatever you say, hearsay. But I didn't see anyone beating anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this -- that it was done by Martic's police, as is stated here, so this information was based on what, presented on the basis of what? Did these people at the barricades say that that is what they were or did they have some kind of insignia? Can you tell us, generally speaking, on the basis of what it was claimed that it was Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I told you, I didn't see them. It was hearsay, as people call it, but that's what was being said. I don't know. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that during the summer of 1991 officers of the JNA came to Saborsko and assured you that there would be no problems between the JNA and the population of Saborsko. Do you remember that statement and that happening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that they came after the shelling and that they gave you such assurances but that you didn't exactly trust them.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When a question was put to you by the Prosecutor in relation to the reinforcements brought in by the JNA and in relation to the reinforcements provided to the Serb units around Saborsko, you stated that it seemed to you that the JNA was bringing in reinforcements and that members of Martic's police were in the area of Licka Jasenica. You said that that is what it seemed like to you. Did you have any more specific knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that from Saborsko you could see only part of JNA training grounds and a few tanks that were there. Was that JNA training grounds in the territory of Saborsko or was it some other training grounds?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Before, it was the territory -- I mean the people were from Saborsko, and they moved out because -- I don't know when, in 1964 or whatever year it was, they were moved out of there. And of course appropriate payments were made and then the military grounds were expanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these training grounds that you mentioned just now, do you know the existence of large military training grounds in Slunj?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's it, from Slunj to Saborsko, military training grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that from Saborsko you could see part of the military training grounds and a few JNA tanks, you were actually referring to the big JNA training grounds near Slunj, which included the reserve command post of the 5th Army; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know who it was and what command, whatever, but I know that that is where military training grounds were and that that is where military training took place beforehand. Now, what was going on then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether near Saborsko -- or rather, in Licka Jasenica there was JNA barracks and a big fuel depot?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not Licka Jasenica, it's in the forest where the railroad is, where the train goes to Split, and that is where the JNA barracks were, up there, with the reservoirs of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described the position of these barracks. Was it a big barrack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is where there were guards before, but then I don't know for what purposes it was used later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that there, near Licka Jasenica, there was a JNA barracks and also a big fuel depot.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And a railroad went to that place, so that is probably why it was there, for transportation purposes, and that there was a JNA unit there.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about attacks against that unit during the course of 1991 and these barracks, conditionally speaking, in Licka Jasenica and where the depot of fuel was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were -- when they were firing at Saborsko, then these people with mortars, this war unit that was there -- well, I don't know who was there exactly at the hill, and that is where the shells were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this detail a little later. Now, I'll remind you of part of your statement that had to do with the shelling of the 5th of August, 1991, the shelling of Saborsko. On the 5th of August, 1991, you explained that in Saborsko, apart from this regular police station where there were 32 of you policemen, there was also a unit of the special police from Duga Resa. Was this a unit of the Croatian special police?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was referring to the Croatian police, but they were not close to the police station. They were in a school about a kilometre and a half away from the police building. They were in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, if you remember, what the make-up of this unit was and how they were armed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them standing there in front of the school and standing guard with automatic rifles. I don't know what they had inside or whether they had anything, but they probably didn't have anything because in the evening they fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer to -- you didn't answer as to how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 30, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: About 30. You explained that on the 5th of August the shelling started and that during the night, together with that unit of the Croatian special police from Duga Resa, the women and children left Saborsko. Were there also elderly people who left the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They went to Grabovac. That's what I said. They went to Grabovac, and from Grabovac the elderly women and children went to Korenica in the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many women, children, and elderly on that evening of the 5th of August, 1991, left Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They all went -- everybody went to Grabovac, and then in Grabovac as many people as could get onto three buses left; 150, 200, I don't know the exact number. I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that women, children, elderly women left Saborsko after this attack and went to Grabovac, and then you described what happened later on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those who hadn't left returned to Saborsko on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody told these people to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the Red Cross or someone or anyone. I don't know because I wasn't in Grabovac. I remained in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me -- or rather, my question was not precise enough. When those women and children set out from Saborsko, did someone from Saborsko elsewhere tell them to go and be evacuated or did they set out on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think they did so on their own initiative because from Licka Jasenica there was mortar fire from the direction of the barracks and also from the direction of Licka Jasenica. The people were afraid. They thought the attack would escalate and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that these policemen from the special police units of Croatia, from Duga Resa, who, as you say, fled that evening, that they were accommodated in the school, and you explained that the school was about a kilometre away from the police station in Saborsko. What other buildings were there near the school? Where was the municipal building? Where was the church?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no municipal building. There was what was called the local commune. That was close to the police station. And there was a shop and an inn there, and there was a school in the middle of Saborsko, there was a post office, and the church was lower down in the direction of Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there an industrial zone in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that on the next day, on the 6th of August, 1991, when these special-purpose policemen from the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia left Saborsko, the specials from Duga Resa, you went to Slunj and that a unit of the special police arrived from Slunj which stayed for about ten days. How many of those men were there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact number. I don't know, but there weren't many. Maybe 15 or 20, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when they arrived, where were they quartered?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They -- some of them remained in Kuselj, near Plitvica, because there were some of them up there, and then six or seven went in another direction, and then some went towards Licka Jasenica. So this position was actually spread out in order to be strengthened if there was a major attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Some 10 or 12 days later, as you said, police from Drezni Grad arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there and where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all in a house, in a house, to be there if they were needed. And that's the same police administration, Karlovac. They came to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Chamber was shown a map more than once during this trial where Saborsko can be seen. If you look at that map, you can see Poljanak, Kuselj, Saborsko, then Plaski --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Licka Jasenica, Blato, Poljcegrad [phoen], Blaga, Plavska Glava, Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
