utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, you have helped me, but I wanted to ask you the following: Could one say that Saborsko is a village that stretches a few kilometres along the road?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Saborsko have any hamlets? Are there any parts of the village, like Borik, Funtana, Panjici, Kuselj, Tuk, Brdine? Is all this part of Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Kuselj to Borik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Alan Height, does it belong to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Mali Sivnik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the middle of Saborsko, towards the military training ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Saborsko stretches lengthwise some 7 kilometres. If one can speak of the breadth of the village, how wide is it, approximately? Can you estimate that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The road runs through Saborsko and some hamlets have a street. So that's maybe half a kilometre more, but all the other houses are lined up along the road, but there are some hamlets to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. You explained about this police force, the special police from Slunj and then the one from Drezni Grad, that they were -- that their disposition was along some lines. Were there men in all of these places, Borik, Funtana --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not in Funtana because it's 2 or 3 kilometres from Kuselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Funtana?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Funtana, yes. There's some water there and that's what it's been called since time immemorial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any in Tuk?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's towards the military training ground, and Borik is to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the hamlet of Brdine?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these specials and your forces deployed in Alan and Mali Sivnik? Those are two different elevations.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but just four or five men. Four or five in Sivnik and four or five in the other place, and in Kuselj there were more because there was a wood there. And where the military training ground was, there was just some who would tell the others if anything happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you became the chief of police in Saborsko on the 20th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the chief, maybe that's an error. Slavko Ceranic was the commander there, and for some family reasons he had to go to Ogulin because he came from Josip -- well, from Ogulin in fact. And then he said to me: You stay here, and he left me the car and the communication equipment and told me to stay there until either he or somebody else came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To repeat your words, you became the commander of that police outpost. Can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I was the commander. I was a policeman, but Slavko left me there and told me to look after the communications and to go to get ammunition in Slunj if need be, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If we describe your position, would I be wrong in saying that as Slavko left, you were his deputy at that post while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was standing in for him until somebody else arrived. They would have to go through Glibodol and through the forest and come back instead of Slavko, because I wasn't really up to that kind of work then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were describing the attack of the 3rd of September, 1991, you said that reserve policemen were wounded, Milan Matovina and Martin Grbic. Where were they at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Between Strkovi and Borik. Those are two hamlets. They were right in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that on the 6th of September, 1991, on the Saborsko-Plitvica road, Ivica Matovina and Marko Sebalj, members of the ZNG, were killed. Stipe Matovina, a reserve Croatian policeman, and another policeman was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Conjar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say they were on the road. Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in the ZNG, Marko Sebalj and the others, and they were going from Grabovac. I don't know. And they came home and then they couldn't go back to Zagreb through Crnjak, and they were members of the ZNG. I don't know where, whether in Zagreb or in Duga Resa where the headquarters was. And they came in a van and they were unable to go back. They could only go as far as Slunj but they couldn't go on to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just another short question: The ZNG, or the National Guards Corps, what was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like an army. What would I know? Like an army. It wasn't the police. It was an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whose army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think now is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, those six people who were killed on the 6th of September, 1991, on the way to Saborsko and Plitvica, we have mentioned their names. You said that they were all in uniform, and in your written statement to the OTP it says they were in olive-grey uniforms, whereas later on you corrected this and said they were actually in camouflage uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these men were armed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had automatic and semi-automatic rifles. I don't know which kind -- you mean those four who were in the van? There were four of them in the van, not six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And those four in the van, when were they killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When they were going from Plitvica, that is from Grabovac on the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Matovina, Marko Sebalj, Stipe Matovina, and another one.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mile Conjar; there were four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, my mistake. So it was four men, not six. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We saw that these men were armed and in uniform. Before that, were civilians killed in a similar manner? Did things like this happen to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no. No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We mentioned the villages of Glibodol -- Glibodol, Saborsko, Ogulin, Dreznik. Were there any Croatian police forces in those villages and were there any members of the ZNG there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I know there was a police station in Drezni Grad. The station was in Slunj, there was an outpost in Drezni Grad. As for Glibodol, I don't know what there was on that side towards Brinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 25th of September, 1991, a convoy of over a hundred men arrived in Saborsko, and these were men who originated in Saborsko. You explained that they were reserve policemen and that they were led by Marko Krizmanic, who was the commander of the Saborsko war unit after that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not after that. He brought them there and he was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that that first convoy, which arrived with over a hundred armed men, brought even mortars and a -- an anti-aircraft weapon. Was that a Browning by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been a Browning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we say "a Browning," would I be right in saying that this is an anti-aircraft machine-gun with a calibre of 12.7 millimetres, of American make?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't actually see it. People just talked about it being there, and I don't know what its calibre was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This convoy of over a hundred armed men, what kind of vehicles did it arrive in from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Trucks. I don't know how many trucks there were. And the food-stuffs, the flour and the cigarettes were loaded onto the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this convoy of armed men with arms and weapons went around the barracks in Licka Jasenica. Why?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't pass through Licka Jasenica, but there's a forest road above the barracks passing through Javornik and then coming down again. It's a forest road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you explained that they couldn't pass through Licka Jasenica, this convoy with armed men. Is that because there was a JNA barracks there, to avoid a conflict with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we from Saborsko couldn't go through Licka Jasenica. How could they go through? They would have gone that way had they believed they could get through, but Saborsko was surrounded on all sides, so they couldn't, and they had to take a shortcut through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that this convoy of the 21st of September, 1991, brought with it nine captured men. One was elderly, the others were younger, and that you recognised two of them as former policemen. And you said they were in camouflage uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had jeans, but the top part of their clothing was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you that. What do you mean when you say "jeans"? Can you describe what these trousers looked like?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the jeans camouflaged or were they normal, civilian jeans?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Normal jeans, just jeans; denim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So these men who were wearing ordinary trousers had multi-coloured jackets?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 2001, it says that they wore camouflage uniforms. Now we see that these were not uniforms. Am I right? They were wearing civilian trousers and multi-coloured jackets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. When did I make that statement that they were in camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 2001. Its number is 03047121, and in English it's 01098817. And on page 3 of that statement -- on page 3, it says, in the last paragraph: "I recognised some of the prisoners, Dusko Jovicic and Damir Vorkapic, policemen from Ogulin." And then it goes on to say: "They were wearing camouflage uniforms," and what I'm asking you is whether what you say today is correct or whether it's what is said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it may be an error but they did have camouflage jackets. The upper part was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were they wearing caps?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they had on when they were captured, but this war unit of Saborsko brought them to the police station outpost in Saborsko like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When answering the Prosecutor's questions today as to whether anything was written on this upper part, multi-coloured top, you said that there was a two-headed eagle, an eagle.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On one side, and I couldn't go into the room because Marko Krizmanic was talking to them and I don't know who else. And then nobody else was supposed to enter the room -- or rather, the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, it doesn't only say that they were in camouflage uniforms, it also says that you said that they had insignia that said "SAO Krajina." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw the insignia and I think that's what it said -- well, it's not that I saw it exactly, but I thought that was that. I mean, what other kind of insignia could they have? It couldn't be the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said that there was a coat of arms on the sleeve. Did you see or assume that it said "SAO Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, if I stood over there and if I'm here, of course you can see that one side but you cannot see the other side, you see. I was standing at the door, like there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, then, if I say that you can confirm that you saw only the eagle?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just part of it. And what about the text "SAO Krajina," did you see it or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on that day, the 25th of September, 1991, with this over 100 armed men, Marko Krizmanic came as commander of the war unit of Saborsko and that he was questioning these nine men who were prisoners and that with him was Luka Hodak, president of the Crisis Staff, as well as the deputy commander of the war unit, Josip Sabljak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Luka Hodak, who you mentioned here, was president of what Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't go into that. It all came from Zagreb, I mean what they did and how this went. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This convoy that we've been talking about all along headed by Commander Marko Krizmanic as commander of the war unit Saborsko, when it arrived in Saborsko, where were these armed men sent to, deployed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all around, as you mentioned: Sivnik, Alan, Kuselj. Part of them went to Borik and Strk. He deployed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Did the commander of that war unit, Marko Krizmanic, work out this deployment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that a few days later these ethnic Serbs were exchanged for three persons from Slunj of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Drezni Grad. It belongs to the municipality of Slunj, but it was Drezni Grad. Perhaps it was written wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I made a mistake in my question. Sorry. Today is -- well, that is what you said today. Anyway, on that day members of Martic's police caught a Croatian policeman and two members of the war unit that were exchanged in December 1991. However, in your statement to the OTP you say that they -- that it was members of Martic's police that captured them. And today when answering questions, you said you didn't know who captured them.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what was being said, that it was either Martic's people or somebody else, but who actually captured them is something I don't know exactly -- well, not even now. I never asked even later. I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP you also say that at the beginning of October 1991, in a conflict between a group of Chetniks and a reconnaissance group of the Saborsko war unit, six members of that Saborsko war unit were wounded. What do you mean by "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, that's what people were saying, that the village was attacked and then this waiter from Plitvica -- well, anyway, that is what people were saying, "Now Cedo is going to show you what he knows." Now, I don't know how it all turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was an armed clash and that in the area of Sertic Poljana there was a clash between these Chetniks, as you called them, with the reconnaissance group of the Saborsko war unit and that several persons were wounded that time. And all of them were members of the war unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in the clash between the reconnaissance group of the Saborsko war unit in the area of Sertic Poljana with a group of Chetniks, several members of the reconnaissance group were wounded, does that mean that these people who you called Chetniks were armed and that this was an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They attacked towards Kuselj and then the reconnaissance men were there and then they called -- well, I don't know, I wasn't there at Kuselj. I just know what they said. When these men were wounded, they were brought to the centre in Saborsko and again people went through the forest to Slunj with the wounded men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned this convoy that arrived on the 25th of September, 1991, from Zagreb, you said that they were reserve policemen of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, that they were all armed, that they brought mortars along, anti-aircraft machine-guns, and that they took up combat positions in Saborsko and around Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Around Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Do you know who armed these 120 reserve policemen? Who gave them mortars? Who gave them these anti-aircraft machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know how this went. They came from Zagreb. I have no idea. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that they were members of the reserve force of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, would it be logical to conclude that they were armed by the Croatian authorities, not by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. When we say "the other side," what do we mean by the other side? Who armed the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in October 1991 another convoy with ammunition and equipment arrived in Saborsko. You said that manpower had not arrived then, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. It's not that 150 men came, but the drivers came driving the trucks and, I don't know, a few security people, I don't know how many there were, who were providing security for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This convoy of trucks, how many trucks did it involve? How big was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know; six or seven, but that's what it was called, the convoy's coming. Now whether it was six or seven, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this convoy was escorted by armed security, about 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who were they; members of the Croatian police or the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reserve police. They had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did this work uniform look like?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was sort of this colour, this colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can that be called a greyish-bluish colour?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, greyish-blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see blue. I see grey only on that jersey. You call that grey-blue, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness to describe this colour for us. When he says "like this," I cannot describe it. But then since he insists on this descriptive answer, I've been trying to interpret it. But that is my question to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe this colour? Did I make a mistake when I said what I said?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's sort of grey. Greyish-bluish, that's what it is, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it one colour or can it be said that it was a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, one colour, the trousers and the top part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The escort of this convoy of 20 men, Croatian reserve policemen, were they armed? And if so, what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Rifles. Some had automatic, some had semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this escort leave with the convoy -- or rather, did the convoy stay in the village or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These armed men, where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed there, as far as I can remember. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your answers to one of my questions you said in relation to the gun-fire opened at JNA barracks on Licka Jasenica that this was a response to their attack. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this was before Saborsko was taken or before it fell, as you say, on the 12th of November, 1991? Was it before that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this was in the period between summer and that date when Saborsko fell?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, summer and this period. I mean, how can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Let us not speak at the same time. I'm asking you whether this was between the period of July/August up to November, because I would like to put this within a time-frame, if possible, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was later, when these people came from Zagreb. Now, when, what date, I don't know. It's after the 25th of September. After the 25th of September. Now, what date it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at a crossroads called Glibodolski Kriz, near Saborsko, three members of the Territorial Defence at Plaski were killed. Do you know of something like that happening in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is the first I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At this intersection they were killed and they were thrown into a pit and it was Susnjar Vasic Stevo, also Susnjar Djure Milan, and Petrovic Milan Bogdan, and a horse's corpse was thrown at their corpses into the pit. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. On the other side, near Brinje, that's where the line was. I don't know, I don't know. Glibodol is far away from Saborsko. You have to walk through the forest. We have no business there except in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think the witness had said to you: I don't know, I'm hearing this for the first time today. When you persist with questions along the same topic, how do you expect him to know anything or give any answer on that? He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have finished my questions. I just wanted to jog the witness's memory, to see whether this would help him remember, but I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He doesn't say he forgot, he says he does not know, he's hearing of it for the first time today. There's no memory to jog here, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that after these reinforcements came, this first convoy with about 120 armed policemen from Zagreb, there was this attack on the Licka Jasenica barracks. There are documents in which the then-JNA recorded what happened and when. Then it is recorded that on the 5th of November and the 7th of November fire was opened from the area of Alan, Veliki Sivnik, at the barracks in Jasenica, and that 26 artillery shells were fired in response. And, for example, a mortar and Browning opened fire at the barracks in Licka Jasenica -- sorry, I misspoke. From the Saborsko side, from Bozin Vrh [phoen]. Then it says that on the 7th of November there was a very strong attack from Saborsko and Glibodol at this barracks from 2.50 in the morning, and it was repelled only at 2000 hours in the evening. Do you know anything about these events?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this did happen, but when the mortars were shooting -- well, they cannot shoot from Sivnik, really. From Alan, yes, but not from Sivnik, but that's the other side. But I know about Alan, yes, I know that that was heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand what you're saying, that you heard mortars from Alan firing at the Licka Jasenica barracks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before that, from Licka Jasenica they were firing, and from the railroad. From the barracks, that is, they were firing at Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were not there when Saborsko fell on the 12th of November, 1991, you were not in Saborsko, did you hear that there was an order issued by the commander of the 5th Army District, Colonel-General Zivota Avramovic, giving an assignment to Tactical Group 2 of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was commanded by Colonel Cedomir Bulat, that on that day, the 12th of November, it should carry out combat operations in the region of Saborsko with the objective of defeating armed enemy groups in that area. Do you know of this order? Have you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that attack at the region of Saborsko against these fortified positions, there was -- there were air strikes, there was artillery and tanks involved, and that this was fierce fighting that ended only in the afternoon. Have you heard anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go into all of this hearsay. I was not there and I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 you entered the new Croatian police. You said that you were asked to sign a statement of loyalty to Martic's police. Do you know whether the Croatian police, established by the new Croatian authorities, asked for policemen of Serb ethnicity to sign such a statement of loyalty to the Croatian police? Have you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Those who had worked in the police before in Ogulin, some stayed and others went to Plaski or Vojnica or wherever they were from, but quite a few of them remained, and now they're retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in early 1991 the Croatian leadership issued a decision that members of the Ministry of the Interior should be called "policija" and that they carried the chequer-board insignia. Do you know when the ZNG was established?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice when we were discussing these events that in many places the Saborsko war unit was deployed and that this was a unit armed and equipped by either the police or the military leadership of the Republic of Croatia and that they were sent to the Saborsko area, which is between the largest military training ground of the former JNA, which was in Slunj, the largest on the territory of Yugoslavia, and Licka Jasenica, where there was a huge fuel depot. Did you notice any connection? Any cause and effect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I didn't understand your question. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask yourself how come the Saborsko war unit, in September 1991 on the territory of the European state of Yugoslavia, between -- was deployed between two very important facilities of the federal armed force? Did you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't think about that. Somebody sent them from Zagreb. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information at the disposal of the Defence - and these are written materials obtained from the Prosecution - during the operation near Saborsko which was carried out at the order of authorised military commanders with the aim of defeating enemy armed forces, the air force artillery tanks of the JNA clashed with armed forces in Saborsko. Do you know how intense the fighting in Saborsko was at the time? Did you hear anything about this later, as you were not there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that there was infantry as well, nothing else. Tanks, planes, artillery, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your replies.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ms. Richterova, any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have only few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, you testified that you heard rumours that Martic's police would stop people at the check-points and beat them. You emphasised that you only heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was it you heard about this beating of people at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ogulin, when I was working there in March. But that's hearsay, I cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From citizens. People were talking about it, but it was just rumours, hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In cross-examination you also were asked questions about ZNG. Were any members of ZNG present and fighting in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, only those two who arrived. I don't know where they had been. When they came home to Saborsko - one of them was from Drezni Grad, his name was Sebalj, he was from somewhere around Plitvica - they came home and couldn't go back in the van. They got as far as Slunj and they couldn't go on. They had to come back. They had only come home for a visit for two or three days, however they were unable to go, to leave again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were, in your opinion, some were from Duga Resa or from Zagreb. Can you assist the Judges and tell us where Duga Resa is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Near Karlovac. I don't know how far; 6 or 7 kilometres, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just to assist the Judges, on the page 20, in the middle of that page you will see Karlovac, and just one centimetre below is Duga Resa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also testified during the cross-examination that those people who left Saborsko at night on 1st -- on 5th of August, that most of them left Saborsko and went towards Rakovica and further and that they left from Rakovica on three buses, those who fit in these buses. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how it was. I wasn't there myself, but that's what I know about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did happen to people who didn't fit to the buses? You testified before that many of them returned, so are you referring to the same people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Those who returned were those who didn't want to go, who were in good health. Those who left were the elderly, the sick, the children, women, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who left -- who returned to Saborsko? Were there -- those who returned to Saborsko, were there among them, were there women, children, elderly people, or did they all left?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some elderly people came back from Grabovac. My parents, for example, and some others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, right at the beginning of your evidence you were asked about relations between Croats and Serbs in the areas that you were testifying about, and you said in response to the question: What changed the relationships? You said: There was no change, it was just a cut off. My question to you is: Are you able to tell what precipitated the cut off?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That's a political matter, perhaps. I don't know who they had there or what they had, and they wouldn't let us use the road and pass through on the bus, and then we couldn't travel. We always got on well in Licka Jasenica, and Saborsko as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who wouldn't let you use the road?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. At ten past 5.00 in the morning, the bus set out for Ogulin, it was the regular line, and it came back. Who it was, I don't know. The bus driver then took the bus through Slunj towards Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From your own observation, what happened to people from your own village who were not travelling by bus but were -- but were using other means of transport? Were they also blocked on the road?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't go towards Ogulin through Jasenica. We didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you don't know why the bus returned. Why did you not go anywhere now on your own?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No one went because the bus was sent back. They -- it couldn't go through. I don't know who stopped it from going, but it came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say I know when I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. Are you aware -- let me ask you differently. Are you aware of people who used some other transport to try and go to Ogulin who were stopped?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know this area that we have been testifying about. There's quite a number of villages that you referred to that you said were attacked. Let me start with your own village where you were born, Saborsko. It was attacked at some stage, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many exactly. The police commander wrote it all down, how many attacks there were, everything, but it all remained behind and it's all been burnt. And now I don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But was it more than once?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was being attacked all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When all the attacks had taken place, what was the condition of the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Those houses that were made of wood were all burnt down. Those that were made of brick or stone were destroyed, and only shells of walls remained. The school, the church, the community club, the post office; everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The entire village had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the people who were in the village at the time of attack, do you know if any one of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilians, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The last attack, I don't know the number but I can say approximately: Three in one place, seven in another, five in yet another place. That's how they were buried when we came in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In your evidence I think you referred -- I don't know whether this is with respect to Saborsko, but you referred to some people who were allegedly thrown into a pit. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Saborsko, yes. My father is there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were thrown in this pit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I know there was seven on one side and I don't know how many on the other side; 13 perhaps, or 12, I can't be sure. They were all thrown in together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like some water?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you okay? Can I carry on asking questions or would you like to take a rest?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can go on, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate it. In other villages -- or let me ask this question: Which -- apart from Saborsko, which are the other villages that you are aware of that were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Poljanak, Sertic Poljana, Drezni Grad, Sebise, Grabovac. I don't know what order it happened in after Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know the extent of damage that was -- that took place at Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't even know the extent of deaths that took place there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about Poljanak. I can't say I know if I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Sertic Poljana?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That fell before Saborsko. There were about 10 or 12 houses there - I don't know exactly how many - and I think that a woman was burned alive in her house, an elderly woman. She was over 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say there were about 10 or 12 houses, that was before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you seen this village since the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you saw it in 1995. Were all the houses still standing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no houses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Drezni Grad, do you know anything --

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Drezni Grad. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't go there. Sebise?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean "no"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go there. I didn't go to look. There was no need for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about Grabovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did go to Grabovac, to the petrol station there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the condition when you got there, after the attack on Grabovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Some houses had been torched, burnt, the motel as well. Some had been destroyed, but there was still some houses standing. Some were intact and some had burnt down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you say the majority were still intact or would you say the minority were still intact?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I just went to the petrol station and there weren't so many houses around there, just a motel, and the petrol pump and a restaurant and a few houses along the road. And I looked at those, and some had been burnt down and some not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether at -- when each one of these villages was being attacked, whether the inhabitants had been aggressive toward the attacker before the attack took place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what happened in those places. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Saborsko, do you know whether the inhabitants of Saborsko became aggressive and caused the attacker to attack Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how. I didn't hear anybody say anything provocative. I didn't hear that ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you at any stage injured in any of these things, activities that took place, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not -- I was not wounded in Saborsko, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not anywhere else either?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ogulin, I stepped on a land-mine. That was in 1991, after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you injured as a result?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In my left leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to show us? Do you mind showing us?

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please see? It looks like the lawyers this side would like to see. Would you like to come this side also to let them see, to show those lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic. We are grateful to you for coming to testify in the court. You -- we're finished -- I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. We are not done with you yet. Ms. Richterova, do you have any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you -- no, it's my mistake. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one question, very briefly, in connection with the wounding in Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness explain to us when in 1991 this happened and what kind of mine it was and who held Ogulin at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Croatian army that was holding it and I was -- I actually stepped on a Croatian land-mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic. Thank you very much. You are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We do not have any witness ready for now, it's only 15 minutes before the break, but we will call another witness on Monday. That will be Vlado Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Very well. Then court will adjourn -- sorry, do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I was just getting up to adjourn. I was just too quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We will adjourn to Monday at 9.00, in the morning. Just to remind you, the whole of next week is 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.42 p.m.,
